The Guyana anchovy Anchoviella guianensis is a small clupeiform fish typical of coastal and estuarine waters of northeastern South America. Field surveys indicate that the maximum total length this species attains is 11.3 cm [Li = 11.3 cm], a size that distinguishes it from several smaller congeners inhabiting similar brackish habitats. The species exhibits a relatively rapid early growth trajectory, with puberty occurring when individuals reach a total length of 5 cm [Lp = 5 cm], a threshold that appears to be reached within the first few months of life. This modest length at sexual maturation likely reflects the selective pressures of a productive but variable environment, where early reproduction can offset high natural mortality rates among young fish. The life cycle from fertilised ovum to reproductively viable adult is compressed, a pattern consistent with many anchovy species that exploit ephemeral plankton blooms. Sexual maturation in this species is thus closely tied to somatic growth rather than chronological age per se, although temperature plays a modulating role in the pace of development across seasons.

At a constant water temperature of 24.5 °C [T = 24.5 °C], the embryonated eggs of Anchoviella guianensis hatch after approximately 2 days [ab = approximately 2 days], a rapid eclosion typical of small teleost eggs with minimal yolk reserves. The newly emerged prolarvae are lecithotrophic and rely entirely on their endogenous yolk supplies during the first few days post-hatching. The wet weight at birth, measured immediately following chorion rupture, is approximately 0.00027 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00027 grams], reflecting the small diameter of the pelagic eggs from which they hatch. This extremely low initial body mass imposes a narrow window for the onset of exogenous feeding; larvae must encounter suitable prey items within hours of yolk-sac resorption to avoid starvation. The timing of this trophic switch is critical for survival and has been linked to local zooplankton density in the species' natural habitat. Such a constrained early life stage is characteristic of many engraulids that produce numerous, small offspring as part of a high-fecundity reproductive strategy.

The ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown adults has been estimated at 13.2 grams [Wwi = 13.2 grams], a value derived from length-weight relationships fitted to field-collected specimens across the species' range. This asymptotic mass is modest even among anchovies, reflecting the relatively small ultimate total length of this species. At the onset of puberty, individuals weigh approximately 0.96 grams [Wwp = approximately 0.96 grams], indicating that a substantial proportion of somatic growth—roughly an order of magnitude in mass—occurs after sexual maturation. This pattern suggests that A. guianensis continues to allocate resources to body growth well into its reproductive life, a common strategy among iteroparous teleosts that face size-dependent fecundity. The disparity between mass at puberty and ultimate mass implies that older, larger females likely contribute disproportionately to population-level egg production. Growth increments slow considerably as individuals approach their asymptotic size, with most mass gain concentrated in the juvenile and early adult stages.

When maintained at a stable temperature of 24.5 °C [T = 24.5 °C], laboratory observations have documented a daily reproduction rate equivalent to approximately 5.5 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 5.5 eggs per day] per female at a standard length of 5.8 cm. This rate was quantified from gravid females held under controlled conditions, where spawning occurred nearly continuously over extended periods. For a female of that body size—corresponding to a total length of roughly 6.7 cm—the observed reproductive output is among the highest recorded for small-bodied engraulids. Such sustained fecundity is energetically demanding and depends on consistent access to planktonic prey. The data suggest that females begin contributing to the next generation almost immediately after reaching puberty and maintain high egg production throughout their reproductively active lifespan. This strategy is adaptive in environments where juvenile mortality is high and unpredictable, favouring maximum current reproduction over the conservation of somatic reserves for future breeding events.

The maximum lifespan documented for Anchoviella guianensis under field conditions is approximately 365 days [am = approximately 365 days] at a water temperature of 24.5 °C [T = 24.5 °C], a longevity that aligns with the annual life cycles typical of many small, fast-growing clupeiforms. This abbreviated lifespan, combined with the high daily reproductive output, characterises a life history strategy that prioritises rapid turnover and numerical abundance over individual survival. Mortality rates are particularly elevated during the pelagic larval phase, when predation pressure from larger planktivores and jellyfish is intense. Among congeneric species, A. guianensis occupies an intermediate position in terms of body size and lifespan, neither as diminutive nor as short-lived as some coastal anchovies, yet far from the larger, longer-lived taxa found in upwelling systems. The species' life cycle is thus tightly synchronised with seasonal productivity pulses in its estuarine and coastal habitats, ensuring that spawning coincides with peak food availability for both larvae and adults.
